claim.why_it_matters: The PDF prints the identification entry without the separator period after FUNCTION-ID (an ISO typesetting defect in this informative example); the markdown silently repairs it. The transcription is meant to reproduce the PDF, and silently normalising the printed text hides an ISO defect a later reader may need to see - and, conversely, anyone diffing markdown against the PDF finds an unexplained mismatch.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED by direct glyph inspection and pixel measurement of the 300 dpi render (E:/Temp/specrecon/v1073/spec_p1073.png; PDF page 1073 = printed page 1043, Annex D, Figure D.2 'Compilation group sample structure example', following D.6.1.1). Attempts to refute all failed: (1) The period is not merely faint or lost to thresholding. On the SAME line, in the SAME monospace font, the trailing period of 'F-1.' is captured cleanly by the same ink threshold as a 5 px run at x=773-778. A period at the FUNCTION-ID position would have been detected identically. (2) The character cell is genuinely EMPTY, not reflowed. The monospace pitch on this line is 21.75 px with cell 0 origin x=440 ('F' of FUNCTION-ID). Ink runs on the FUNCTION-ID line are: F(440) U(460) N(482) C(504) T(527) I(550) O(570) N(591) -(615) I(637) D(658), then a 25 px stretch of pure white from x=676 to x=701, then F(701) -(724) 1(746) .(773). Cell index 11 (x 680-701) - exactly where the separator period belongs - carries zero ink. (3) The contrast against the sibling line is unambiguous. 'PROGRAM-ID. P-1.' on the same page measures P(440) R(460) O(482) G(504) RA(526-567) M(569) -(593) I(616) D(636) .(664-669, width 5) then space then P(702): the period glyph is plainly present in its cell. Both lines land their name token at cell index 12, but PROGRAM-ID gets there with period+space while FUNCTION-ID gets there with a single space and no period. (4) Not a spacing/alignment artifact. Both PDF comment markers on this construct ('*>' after FUNCTION-ID and after END FUNCTION) begin at x=1009 = column 27; 'FUNCTION-ID F-1.' is 16 characters + 10 spaces = column 27, and 'END FUNCTION F-1.' is 17 characters + 9 spaces = column 27. The claim's quoted PDF spacing (10 spaces) is therefore exactly right, and the markdown's 17 characters + 8 spaces = column 26 is a one-column whitespace shift that is immaterial. (5) The claim misquotes neither source. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 43024 reads verbatim 'FUNCTION-ID. F-1.        *> Source element start' (17 chars + 8 spaces), matching the claim character for character. The substantive delta is a single inserted '.' token. (6) The characterisation as an ISO defect is correct: the normative general format at ISO/IEC 1989:2023 11.5, FUNCTION-ID paragraph (specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 12932) is 'FUNCTION-ID. user-function-name-1 [ AS literal-1 ] .', so the separator period is required and the printed Annex D figure contradicts the standard's own format. 'cosmetic' is the right severity: Annex D is informative, and the markdown's text is the syntactically valid COBOL, so no implementer is misled about semantics - the transcription simply fails to reproduce what the canonical PDF prints.
verdict.corrected_description: Accurate as filed; no correction needed. For the record, the precise delta is the insertion of one separator-period token: PDF page 1073 (printed 1043), Annex D Figure D.2, prints 'FUNCTION-ID F-1.' followed by 10 spaces with the comment at column 27, while specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 43024 transcribes 'FUNCTION-ID. F-1.' followed by 8 spaces with the comment at column 26. The comment-column shift is incidental whitespace; only the added '.' is substantive. Every other identification entry in the same figure (PROGRAM-ID., CLASS-ID., METHOD-ID.) prints its separator period in the PDF, so the FUNCTION-ID line is an isolated ISO editorial slip that contradicts the normative format in 11.5, FUNCTION-ID paragraph. The fix is to restore the PDF's printed text and annotate the line as a known ISO defect rather than silently normalising it.
